SEC-HC-01.note: Two dimensions (crust->anchors; independent clause after 'however' needs semicolon). Not resolvable from after-blank alone: the agreement half needs the subject. Same template as 02 and 03.

SEC-HC-02.note: C and D are fragments ('restorers who cannot...' never gets a main verb); A is a comma splice. Same semicolon+conjunctive-adverb template as 01/03 with the same distractor profile as 03.

SEC-HC-03.note: B and D are obvious fragments, A a comma splice; only one finite-verb option with a semicolon. Near-duplicate of 02 in option architecture (participle / relative pronoun / splice / key).

SEC-HC-04.note: B is the only good distractor (temperatures...falls); D's 'which is:' is not a real convention. Not cued by after-blank.

SEC-HC-05.note: CUED: 'a container of ordinary kitchenware, and a location' fixes the separator as a comma and the items as noun phrases, which kills A (semicolon), B ('such as:' and 'such as' vs 'three'), and C (non-parallel 'that' clause) without reading the stem.

SEC-HC-06.note: Requires parsing 'sparrows raised within earshot of adults reproduce' as the main clause; A and D strip the main verb, C is a comma splice. Colon introducing elaboration is acceptable; a semicolon would be equally natural but is not offered.

SEC-HC-07.note: B and C leave 'whose cores' with no verb; D fails agreement (cores/supplies) and drops 'last'. TYPOGRAPHIC TELL: B and C begin with a comma but the stem has a space before the blank ('cores , which'); the two odd-looking options are both wrong.

SEC-HC-08.note: 'together with' does not pluralize; B (compound subject + singular verb) is the genuine trap, and 'its proportions' later in the stem quietly confirms a singular head. This is the real module-2 shape.

SEC-HC-09.note: Reached by elimination: 'array' is singular, so A fails, and B/C have unbalanced commas. But semantically 'The strait's array' is already fully identified, so a nonrestrictive clause (A's form) is what a careful writer would choose; the key forces a restrictive reading that implies other arrays exist. Same leading-comma typographic tell as 07 ('turbines , whose'). Borderline ambiguous stem.

SEC-HC-10.note: Agreement across 'painters ... ores' plus appositive comma; B's semicolon strands a fragment. Not cued.

SEC-HC-11.note: A vs C is only the closing comma of the parenthetical; B/D are cheap. Not cued.

SEC-HC-12.note: 'Each of the walls' -> has. D (dash) would be fine punctuation but carries the wrong verb, which makes it a decent distractor; C drops 'with age' and strands a fragment.

SEC-HC-13.note: Specific past time ('returned in 2019') rules out present perfect. STEM: 'the ecologist who had warned that trees set out in straight rows would fail reported that' is a garden path ('would fail reported') - grammatical but hard to parse, which adds reading load unrelated to the tested convention.

SEC-HC-14.note: 'Since ... 1930s' requires present perfect; B (simple past) is heard in speech but not edited standard. Not cued.

SEC-HC-15.note: 'had already showed' and 'have already shown' are cheap eliminations; only C competes, and 'By the time ... were released' strongly signals past perfect.

SEC-HC-16.note: Classic 'who [records say] trained' trap; A (whom) is the hypercorrection strong students choose. CUED (mostly): 'trained the next generation' after the blank settles who/whom by itself; only ruling out C ('which') needs the antecedent 'apprentice', and D fails internally ('records says').

SEC-HC-17.note: Two cases in one blank: object of 'between' (him) and subject of 'had first noticed' (who); C is the genuine trap. he/him needs the words before the blank, so not resolvable from after-blank alone.

SEC-HC-18.note: Object-of-'to' pull toward whomever vs subject of 'could keep'. CUED: ', in its own judgment, could keep' after the blank determines whoever and kills C's double subject; this is inherent to the whoever/whomever type, not an authoring defect.

SEC-HC-19.note: 'predicts' kills A; B and D dangle the opening participle (D's cleft attaches 'Trained' to 'it'). Same option architecture as 20 and 21 (plural / singular / relative fragment / expletive).

SEC-HC-20.note: A fails agreement (tablet/survive), C is a fragment, D dangles onto 'there'. Structural near-duplicate of 19.

SEC-HC-21.note: A vs D differ only in 'waters'/'water' against 'preserves'; legitimate but thin. B removes the subject, C is a fragment. Structural near-duplicate of 19/20.

SEC-HC-22.note: Paired dashes must close with a dash (C fails), the series is gerunds (B fails), the sentence needs a finite verb (D fails). 'the sessions their unusual warmth' after the blank kills only D.

SEC-HC-23.note: Either repeat 'in' for every item or for none; A mixes. B fails agreement (Geneticists/has), D puts a comma between subject and verb. Not cued.

SEC-HC-24.note: Series is bare infinitives after 'had to'; D's stray 'to' breaks parallelism, A is a gerund, C splices. 'the whole sequence must finish' after the blank kills only C.
